'''T. Kurtis<ref name="GEEA">{{cite journal|url=http://geea.lyellcollection.org/content/17/4/277 |journal=Geochemistry: Exploration, Environment, Analysis |title=T. Kurtis Kyser (1951–2017) |author=Ryan Noble, Dan Layton-Matthews and Matt Leybourne. |date=2017 |volume=17 |issue=4 |doi=10.1144/geochem2017-905 |pages=277–278 |bibcode=2017GEEA...17..277N |s2cid=134344373 |accessdate=March 1, 2019|url-access=subscription }}</ref> (Kurt) Kyser''' (October 7, 1951,<ref name="GSL">{{cite web|url=https://www.geolsoc.org.uk/Geoscientist/Archive/November-2017/Kurt-Kyser-dies-at-62 |title=Kurt Kyser dies at 65 |publisher=[[The Geological Society of London]]|accessdate=March 1, 2019}}</ref> [[Montana]], U.S. — August 29, 2017, [[Bermuda]]) was an American and Canadian geologist and geochemist, Fellow of the [[Royal Society of Canada]], professor of the [[University of Saskatchewan]] and [[Queen's University at Kingston|Queen's University]], founder and director of the Queen's Facility for Isotope Research (QFIR). Kyser served as a president of the Mineralogical Association of Canada (between 2006 and 2008) and as an Editor-in-Chief of the journal ''[[Geochemistry: Exploration, Environment, Analysis]]'' (GEEA).

== Biography ==
Kurt Kyser was born in 1951 in [[Montana]] and grew up in [[San Diego]], California. As a child, he was interested in entomology, but later he decided that geology is more fascinating for him. In 1974, Kyser graduated from the [[University of California, San Diego]], then proceeding to postgraduate studies at the university [[University of California, Berkeley|branch in Berkeley]], where he finished his MA studies in 1976, and PhD in Geology in 1980.<ref name="GEEA" /> His PhD became a pioneering work on the use of stable isotopes for the study of seafloor basalt.<ref name="Elements">{{cite journal|title=Remembering Dr. Kurt Kyser |author=Eric Hiatt, Peir Pufahl and Ron Peterson. |journal=Elements |date=2017 |volume=13 |issue=6 |issn=1811-5217 |pages=424 |doi=10.3749/canmin.OBIT000005 |bibcode=2018CaMin..56..109H }}</ref>

After completing a post-doctoral fellowship at the [[United States Geological Survey]] in Denver and a NATO post-doctoral fellowship at the [[University of Paris]], Kyser returned to the North America to work at the [[University of Saskatchewan]] (Canada) as an assistant professor; in 1989 he was made a full professor. In 1995 he joined the Department of Geological Sciences and Geological Engineering at [[Queen's University at Kingston|Queen's University]] in Kingston. There, under the guidance of Kyser, the Queen's Facility for Isotope Research (QFIR) was established and became the leading geochemistry and isotope laboratory in North America. Kyser was strongly committed to developing the next generation of geochemists and supervised circa 50 MSc and as many PHD students in the field of geochemistry during his tenure as professor, including 26 MSc and 17 PhD theses just in the second decade of the 2000s.<ref name="GEEA" /> He published over 500 peer-reviewed papers, including book chapters, books and technical reports.<ref name="Elements" /> The bulk of his research focused on application of isotopes, uranium in particular, to mineral exploration and environmental geochemistry, although he was influential on multiple other science disciplines.<ref name="GEEA" />

Kurt Kyser was a member of the Mineralogical Association of Canada (where he served as president from 2006 to 2008), [[Mineralogical Society of America]], [[American Geophysical Union]], Geochemical Society of America and the [[Association of Applied Geochemists]]. During last years of his life he served as the Editor-in-Chief of the [[Geological Society of London]]'s journal ''[[Geochemistry: Exploration, Environment, Analysis]]''.<ref name="Elements" /> He died while snorkeling,<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.royalgazette.com/news/article/20170901/tributes-to-professor-who-died-snorkelling |title=Tributes to professor who died snorkelling |author=Paul Johnston. |work=The Royal Gazette |date=September 1, 2017 |accessdate=March 1, 2019}}</ref> in August 2017 in [[Bermuda]], where he was co-leading an annual field trip on [[carbonate]]s. Kurt was survived by his wife, April Vuletich.<ref name="GEEA" />

== Awards ==
Kurt Kyser was a Fellow of the [[Royal Society of Canada]]. His scientific achievements were recognized by professional awards from the Mineralogical
Association of Canada (Past-Presidents Medal, 2001; Hawley Medal, 2002, 2021), [[Geological Association of Canada]] (Past President’s Medal; Duncan R. Derry Medal, 2017), [[Natural Sciences and Engineering Research Council]] (E.W.R. Steacie Memorial Fellowship), [[Canada Council|Canada Council for the Arts]] (Killam Research Fellowship) and the Royal Society of Canada ([[Willet G. Miller Medal]]).<ref name="Elements" />
